root_cause.evidence: The patch moves `prepare_peercred()` to execute before `unix_create1()`, ensuring that if credential preparation fails, no socket allocation has occurred yet and no cleanup is needed. The original code had `prepare_peercred()` after `unix_create1()` with an error path that jumped to `out` without calling `unix_release_sock(newsk)`, leaving the allocated socket unreleased when credential preparation failed.

bic_trace_step.code_snippet:
commit fd0a109a0f6b7524543d17520da92a44a9f5343c
Author: Christian Brauner <brauner@kernel.org>
Date:   Fri Apr 25 10:11:31 2025 +0200

    net, pidfs: prepare for handing out pidfds for reaped sk->sk_peer_pid
    
    SO_PEERPIDFD currently doesn't support handing out pidfds if the
    sk->sk_peer_pid thread-group leader has already been reaped. In this
    case it currently returns EINVAL. Userspace still wants to get a pidfd
    for a reaped process to have a stable handle it can pass on.
bic_trace_step.reason: This commit introduces the fix for the vulnerability described in the root cause. The vulnerability was that `prepare_peercred()` (formerly called after socket allocation) could fail without proper cleanup. This commit restructures the code to call `prepare_peercred()` BEFORE socket allocation in critical paths (unix_listen, unix_stream_connect, unix_socketpair), ensuring that if it fails, no socket has been allocated yet and no cleanup is needed. Additionally, the commit adds proper error handling with `drop_peercred()` calls in all error paths (lines 823-824 in unix_listen, line 1748 in unix_stream_connect, and lines 1760-1761 in unix_socketpair). The new `drop_peercred()` function properly cleans up the peercred structure by calling `pidfs_put_pid()` and `put_pid()` on the peer_pid. Furthermore, `unix_sock_destructor()` now includes cleanup code (lines 646-647) that calls `pidfs_put_pid(sk->sk_peer_pid)` when the socket is destroyed, ensuring the pidfs reference is released. The vulnerable construct (calling prepare_peercred after socket allocation without proper cleanup on failure) is not present in this version - the code has been refactored to prevent the vulnerability entirely.

bic_trace_step.reason: This commit introduces a fix for the vulnerability described in the root cause. The vulnerability was that `prepare_peercred()` was called after socket allocation, and if it failed, the socket wasn't properly cleaned up. This commit restructures the code to call `prepare_peercred()` BEFORE the socket is fully committed, and implements proper error handling with `drop_peercred()` cleanup. Specifically: (1) In `unix_listen()`, `prepare_peercred(&peercred)` is called at line 821-823 before `unix_state_lock()`, and `drop_peercred(&peercred)` is called at line 838 in the error path. (2) In `unix_stream_connect()`, `prepare_peercred(&peercred)` is called at lines 1610-1612 early in the function, and `drop_peercred(&peercred)` is called at line 1748 in the error path. (3) In `unix_socketpair()`, both `prepare_peercred()` calls are made at lines 1755-1765 with proper error handling and cleanup via `drop_peercred()` before any socket state is modified. The new `drop_peercred()` function (lines 761-772) properly cleans up both the pidfs reference and the pid/cred references. Additionally, `unix_sock_destructor()` now calls `pidfs_put_pid()` at lines 647-648 to ensure cleanup when the socket is destroyed. This ensures that if `prepare_peercred()` fails, the error path properly cleans up via `drop_peercred()` before the socket is used.
